title: One neuron, one line
instruction: Set the weights and the threshold so that the line separates two groups of points. The neuron says “second group” when weight₁ · x + weight₂ · y is greater than the threshold.

levels.story: A pet recogniser knows an animal’s weight and height. Separate the cats from the dogs.
levels.why: One feature is enough: the dogs here are heavier. If you set the weight for height to zero, the line is vertical and it still works.

levels.story: A spam filter counts exclamation marks and links. Neither feature is enough on its own. Find a slanted line.
levels.why: Spam has lots of exclamation marks and links together. Both weights must be positive and roughly equal, with the threshold between 6 and 7. Using just one feature, you’ll reach about 79% at most.

levels.story: A micro:bit tells waving from clapping by the strength and speed of the movement. But two recordings went wrong. Try for 100%.
levels.why: 100% isn’t possible: two points lie in the middle of the other group. The best line gets 12 out of 14, which is 86%. Don’t chase bad data. The only way to fix it is to record those movements again.

levels.story: A staircase light switch: the light is on when one switch is up and the other is down. The axes show the position of the bottom and the top switch (0 = down, 10 = up). Can one neuron learn this?
levels.why: The “on” points are in two opposite corners. One line can’t separate them from the “off” points; the best you can get is 6 out of 8. This is called the XOR problem. You need two neurons and a third one that combines their results. That’s the hidden layer of a neural network.

debrief: One neuron can do only one thing: draw a straight line. Where a line is enough, it learns quickly. Where the data lies, 100% isn’t possible. And where more lines are needed, another layer of neurons is added. Whole neural networks are just lots of these lines stacked on top of each other.
